```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Hierarchical ccupancy and abundance models that account for imperfect detection of 
wildlife require two things from camera trap data: a **detection history** (was the
species detected at each site on each sampling occasion?) and the **sampling effort**
behind it (how long were cameras running there?). This vignette builds both from a 
WildObs data package, first with camera stations as sites and then across spatially 
resampled hexagonal grid cells. It project 0001, a systematic survey of six Wet Tropics
landscapes shipped with WildObsR, so everything runs offline.

The next vignette, *Fitting occupancy and abundance models*, takes these matrices into
unmarked, spOccupancy, spAbundance and NIMBLE.

## Which function should I use?

| You want to | Use |
|---|---|
| Camera-days per site and occasion, from the deployments alone | `effort_matrix()` |
| Detections that line up exactly with that effort | `detection_matrix()` |
| The format a modelling package expects, with covariates matched by site | `model_matrix_input()` |
| One row of covariates per grid cell | `resample_covariates_and_observations(obs = NULL)` |
| To reproduce an analysis built before WildObsR v0.4 | `matrix_generator()` (legacy) |

In the latest v0.4 release, `effort_matrix()`, `detection_matrix()` and 
`model_matrix_input()` replace `matrix_generator()` for new work. Their 
sampling effort comes from the deployments, so it never depends on where animals
were detected, and they work on any dataset formatted in Camtrap DP.

## Three tables, two keys

Each function takes the table at the level it needs:

| Table | One row per | Goes into |
|---|---|---|
| Deployments | deployment | `effort_matrix()` |
| Observations | observation | `detection_matrix()` |
| Site-level covariates | site | `model_matrix_input(site_covs = )` |

`deploymentID` links observations to deployments, and the site column (`locationID`
here, or a cellID after spatial resampling later) links deployments to sites. Nothing 
needs to be summarised beforehand except the site covariates, because a model needs 
exactly one value per site.

```{r data}
# load the R package 
library(WildObsR)

# grab the the Wet Tropics survey shipped with WildObsR, the first example dataset 
dp <- example_datapackages("ZAmir_QLD_Wet_Tropics_2022_WildObsID_0001")[[1]]

# extract the three tables, read with their schema types
deps <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "deployments")
covs <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "covariates")
obs <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "observations")
# merge deployments and their environmental covariates as one table, based on shared columns
deps <- merge(deps, covs, by = intersect(names(deps), names(covs)))

# verify deployments and covariates didnt change rows
nrow(deps) == nrow(covs) # must be TRUE

# view deployments, camera stations and observations
c(deployments = nrow(deps), stations = length(unique(deps$locationID)), observations = nrow(obs))
```

There are nearly twice as many deployments as stations, because most stations held two
cameras placed on different `featureTypes`. A station is the natural site when cameras 
were placed on purpose at fixed points.

## Sampling effort

`effort_matrix()` splits every deployment into the local calendar days it ran, with the
fraction of each day covered, and sums those camera-days per site and occasion. Here an
occasion is 7 days (`w = 7`) and only the first 70 days at each station are kept
(`dur = 70`), so every station has at most 10 occasions.

```{r effort}
# camera-days per station and 7-day occasion, over each station's first 70 days
eff <- effort_matrix(deps, site_col = "locationID", w = 7, dur = 70,
                    # specify the timezone from temporal metadata in the descriptor 
                     time_zone = dp$temporal$timeZone)

# inspect the number of stations x occasions x deployment slots
dim(eff$effort)
# view the total effort over a station's cameras, for the first four stations
round(eff$effort_total[1:4, ], 1)
```

A full week with both cameras running gives 14 camera-days; a week where one camera
stopped gives 7, and the first week is a little short because cameras were set up during
the day. An occasion of 0 means no camera ran, which happens at the end of a station's
sampling, or in gaps between deployments. Effort is calculated from deployment start and 
end times only, so it is the same for whatever species you later model.

The `occasions` table gives each occasion's dates, and `deployments` says which deployment
sits in which slot of the third dimension:

```{r effort-tables}
# view the dates of each station's occasions
head(eff$occasions, 3)
# view which deployment is in which slot at each station, which links observations
head(eff$deployments, 3)
```

By default each station's occasions start on its own first day (`align = "site"`). With
`align = "calendar"`, occasion `k` covers the same dates at every station, which
multi-season and time-series models need; see *Long-term monitoring series*.

## Detection histories

`detection_matrix()` places every detection on its deployment's site and local day, then
fills the same sites and occasions as the effort. A cell is `NA` where no camera ran and 0
where cameras ran without detecting the species, so a non-detection is never confused
with no sampling.

```{r detections}
# specify three common species of the Wet Tropics rainforest
species <- c("Thylogale stigmatica", "Hypsiprymnodon moschatus", "Sus scrofa")
# create a matrix filled by detected (1) or not (0) per station and occasion
y <- detection_matrix(obs, eff, species)

# view the number of species x stations x occasions
dim(y)
# view red-legged pademelon at the first four stations
y["Thylogale stigmatica", 1:4, ]
```

The messages say what was set aside before counting:

- **Obscured records.** Threatened-species records in public data carry no `deploymentID`,
  so they cannot be placed on a site. Detection histories built from public data may 
  under-count those species where they are listed.
- **Records that are not of animals**, such as blanks, people and vehicles.

A detection on a day its camera was not running stops the function, because it means the
deployment dates and the observations disagree.

### Counts for abundance models

In the `detection_matrix()` function, you can include the parameter `type = "abundance"`,
to produce a count history matrix for modelling abundance, where the `count` field from 
the observations table is used to populate the matrix. Counts are combined in two steps:

1. Within each event (`eventID`, a 30-minute window at one camera), the *largest* `count` is
   the number of animals seen. A single pig that triggers a camera three times in ten minutes
   is counted as one individual. 
2. Events in an occasion are then combined by specifing a function in the `individuals` 
   parameter. `"max"` takes the most animals seen at one occasion, which is the conservative
   option that N-mixture models assume. `"sum"` adds the events, producing a relative abundance
   index, and could count one animal twice if it passes two cameras at a station.

```{r abundance}
# create a abundance matrix for the most feral pigs seen together per station and occasion
n <- detection_matrix(obs, eff, "Sus scrofa", type = "abundance", individuals = "max")
# view the first 4 sites
n["Sus scrofa", 1:4, ]

# compare with the sum number of pigs detected per station and occasion
s <- detection_matrix(obs, eff, "Sus scrofa", type = "abundance", individuals = "sum")
# view the first 4 sites
s["Sus scrofa", 1:4, ]
```

Note, the default behavior of `detection_matrix()` is to generate a detection history matrix,
(*i.e.*, `type = "occupancy"`) not a count history matrix. Make sure to include the parameter 
`type = "abundance"` to generate a matrix for modelling abundance. 

## Detection that depends on where the camera points

Cameras on roads and trails often detect animals at different rates from cameras off
them. `split_by` splits the effort by a deployment column, so the share of each occasion's
camera-days on trail can be used as an observation covariate. In this survey,
`featureType` is empty for cameras placed off trail.

```{r split}
# create a new two-level trail status: any road or trail, or none
deps$trailStatus <- ifelse(is.na(deps$featureType), "offTrail", "onTrail")
# view the new column
table(deps$trailStatus)

# recreate the the same effort matrix, but now split by trail status
eff_trail <- effort_matrix(deps, site_col = "locationID", w = 7, dur = 70,
                          # explicitly define which column is used to split the effort matrix 
                           split_by = "trailStatus", time_zone = dp$temporal$timeZone)
# the third dimension now holds the on vs off trail levels, not the cameras
dimnames(eff_trail$effort)[[3]]
```

`model_matrix_input()` turns the split into observation covariates: `effort` (camera-days)
and one share per level, here `trailStatus_offTrail` and `trailStatus_onTrail`. This survey
paired one camera on a trail with one off it at most stations, so the share on trail is
0.5 while both run, and changes when one of them stops. The shares of a station's levels 
add up to 1, so a model formula uses one of them, for example
`~ effort + trailStatus_onTrail`. It also adds `total_effort`, each station's total camera-days
over the modelled occasions and splits, as a site covariate.

```{r split-covs}
# create the detections for this effort, as plain arrays
inp <- model_matrix_input(detection_matrix(obs, eff_trail, species), eff_trail, output = "array")
# view the observation covariates it adds
names(inp$obs_covs)
# view the share of camera-days on trail at the first four stations
round(inp$obs_covs$trailStatus_onTrail[1:4, 1:5], 2)
# do the same for off trail
round(inp$obs_covs$trailStatus_onTrail[1:4, 1:5], 1)
```

`split_by` takes one column. To split by two, combine them into one first, for example
`paste(deps$baitUse, deps$trailStatus, sep = "_")`.

## Grid cells as sites

When cameras were not placed at fixed points, or when projects with different designs are
pooled, a regular grid makes a common site. `spatial_hexagon_generator()` assigns every
deployment to a hexagonal cell. **The scale is a cell area in square metres**, so `3e6`
gives 3 km² cells; `3000` would give cells about 60 m across. The 
`spatial_hexagon_generator()` function can generate many different hexagonal cells with one call
by specifying multiple areas in the `scales` paramater. 

```{r cells}
# assign every deployment to both 3 km2 and 6 km2 hexagonal cells
deps_cellID <- spatial_hexagon_generator(deps, scales = c(3e6, 6e6))
# ensure its still one row per deployment, but now with two different cellIDs
c(deployments = nrow(deps_cellID), 
  # expect to see less cells as area increases 
  cells_3km2 = length(unique(deps_cellID$cellID_3km2)),
  cells_6km2 = length(unique(deps_cellID$cellID_6km2)))
```

Effort and detections are built using exactly the same function as before, with cellID specified
as the site. The observations need no changes: `detection_matrix()` finds each record's cell
through its `deploymentID` stored in the `deployments` table of the output from `effort_matrix()`.

```{r cell-effort}
# create the sampling matrix filled with camera-days per cell and occasion, split by trail status
eff_cell <- effort_matrix(deps_cellID, site_col = "cellID_3km2", w = 7, dur = 70,
                          split_by = "trailStatus", time_zone = dp$temporal$timeZone)

# create the matrix filled with detections (0/1) per cell and occasion for all species
y_cell <- detection_matrix(obs, eff_cell, species)
# inspect number of species, rows, and columns 
dim(y_cell)
```

The site-level covariates require one value per cell and it does not vary through the sampling 
duration. The function `resample_covariates_and_observations()` uses the cellIDs generated by
`spatial_hexagon_generator()` to spatially resample both the observations and covariates.
Since `detection_matrix()` matches observations via `deploymentID` to fill a detection history
matrix, we only need resampled covariates to match each cell in the matrix. Use 
`resample_covariates_and_observations()` without including the observations (*i.e.*, `obs = NULL`
) to quickly average each cell's numeric covariates, weighting every deployment by its
camera-days, and take the modal value covering the most camera-days for the columns specified in
`mode_cols_covs`. It takes about a second.

```{r cell-covs}
# resample covariates to produce one row of covariates per cellID
cell <- resample_covariates_and_observations(deps_cellID, mode_cols_covs = "trailStatus")
# pull out the resampled covaraites from the returned list 
cell_covs <- cell$spatially_resampled_covariates$cellID_3km2
# inspect a few of them for the first three cells
head(cell_covs[, c("cellEffort", "Avg_altitude_point", "mode_trailStatus")], 3)
```

`cellEffort` is every day each camera in the cell ran, while `total_effort` from
`model_matrix_input()` counts only the modelled occasions, so the two differ when `dur` in
`effort_matrix()` cuts sampling short.

Do not pass the resampled covariates to `effort_matrix()`. When multiple cameras are grouped into
a single cell, each individual cameras' start and end dates have been collapsed to an overall cell
start and end date, which reduces resolution for sampling effort within the cell. If you supply 
resampled covariates to the `effort_matrix()` function, it will stop and says which table to use
instead.

## The legacy route, for comparison

The first matrix function created in WildObsR was `matrix_generator()`, which builds detection
histories from resampled observations. We can compare function from this this survey to confirm
that both routes give the same detection histories, which is a useful check:

```{r legacy}
# subset observations for pademelon records that can be placed on a camera
pademelon <- obs[obs$deploymentID %in% deps_cellID$deploymentID &
                   obs$scientificName == "Thylogale stigmatica", ]
# resampled to cells and days, as matrix_generator() needs
resamp <- suppressWarnings(
  # Note, resampling the observations is slow, takes ~45 seconds. 
  resample_covariates_and_observations(deps_cellID, pademelon, individuals = "max"))

# create hte legacy detection history, over the same 70 days in 7-day occasions
legacy <- suppressWarnings(matrix_generator(
  # specify the resampled observations and covariates 
  obs = resamp$spatially_resampled_observations$cellID_3km2,
  covs = resamp$spatially_resampled_covariates$cellID_3km2,
  # assign the same sampling duration and occassions
  dur = 70, w = 7, 
  # select a single site-level covariate and no observation covariats 
  site_covs = "Avg_altitude_point", obs_covs = character(0),
  # include all landscapes and specify only one species 
  all_locationNames = TRUE, scientificNames = "Thylogale stigmatica",
  # make a matrix for occupancy models
  type = "occupancy"))
# pull out the detection matrix for a closer look
y_legacy <- legacy$Thylogale_stigmatica$detection_matrix

# pull out the new history, in the same row order
y_new <- y_cell["Thylogale stigmatica", rownames(y_legacy), ]
# are the detections the same, and occasions the same without effort
identical(unname(y_legacy == 1), unname(y_new == 1))
```

The difference is in effort. `matrix_generator()` has no camera-days: it treats a cell as
sampled continuously from its first deployment start to its last end, including gaps
between deployments, and its `numberDeploymentsActiveAtDate` counts only the cameras that
recorded something that day. `?matrix_generator` lists these limits. The legacy function
may be deprecated in a future release.

## Choices to make

- **Occasion length (`w`).** Longer occasions raise detection probability per occasion
  and give fewer, less autocorrelated occasions. A week is common for medium-sized mammals.
- **Survey length (`dur`).** Occupancy models assume the population is closed: the population 
  does not increase or decrease at a site during the survey. Cut each site's sampling to a 
  period where that is plausible, based on the biology of your study species. 
- **Site size.** A station suits cameras placed at fixed points with regular spacing between
  points; a grid cell suits pooling cameras with unequal spacing and for species whose home 
  range spans several cameras. The cell area sets what "occupied" means.
- **Time zone.** Days run in the package's time zone (`dp$temporal$timeZone`). When pooled
  cameras span time zones with different clocks, both functions use UTC days instead, with
  a message, so effort and detections still share the same day boundaries.
